title: Edit Distance: the Levenshtein Table, Row by Row
excerpt: How the edit distance recurrence is built, why the three neighbours correspond to delete, insert and replace, and how to collapse the table to two rows.
seoTitle: Edit Distance (Levenshtein) Explained — O(n·m) Dynamic Programming
seoDescription: A walkthrough of the edit distance algorithm: the recurrence, what each of the three neighbouring cells means, the base cases, and the O(min(n,m)) space optimisation.

content.text: Edit distance asks the fewest single-character edits — insert, delete or replace — that turn one string into another. Turning

It is the archetypal two-dimensional dynamic program, and the reason it is worth working through carefully is that the recurrence is short but every term in it means something specific. Getting the meanings straight is most of the work; the code is eight lines.

Define d[i][j] as the distance between the first i characters of the source and the first j of the target. When the current characters match, the cost is whatever d[i-1][j-1] was — a free diagonal step. When they differ, it is one plus the cheapest of three neighbours, and each neighbour corresponds to exactly one edit operation. Only the previous row is ever read, so the table collapses to two rows.

body.text: Complexity, and why the space optimisation is safe

content.text: Every cell is computed once from three constant-time lookups, so the running time is O(n·m). That is optimal in the general case: under the strong exponential time hypothesis no algorithm computes exact edit distance in O((n·m)^(1−ε)) time, so the table is not a stepping stone to something asymptotically better.

body.title: The one thing the two-row version costs you

content.text: Reconstructing the actual edit script needs the whole table, because you have to walk backwards from the corner. If you only want the number, two rows are strictly better; if you want the operations, keep the full table.

items.text: Forgetting the base row and column. A table of zeros yields 0 for every pair of strings, which looks like a subtle bug and is actually a missing initialisation.
Adding one on a match. The diagonal step is free; adding one turns edit distance into something that counts aligned characters.
Reading current[j] instead of previous[j] for the delete case. current[j] has not been written yet on this pass, so the value is stale from two rows ago.
Off-by-one between string indices and table indices. The table is (n+1) x (m+1) and cell [i][j] refers to characters i-1 and j-1.
